h1: How to Plan a Dairy Shed for Pakistan's Heat: Roof, Ridge and Airflow
quickAnswer: A good dairy shed in Pakistan gives shade, lets hot air leave and keeps the floor dry. Plan a high roof, an open ridge, open or louvered sides, an insulated roof where needed and a floor that drains. Steel Mind Engineers has built dairy sheds of 39,330, 22,000 and 21,686 square feet for Dravton Dairy and Latifia Dairy.
alt: Dairy shed design for heat in Pakistan

faq.q: How many animals can a shed hold?
faq.a: It depends on the area per animal and the layout. The engineer plans the width and length from your herd size.

faq.q: Is a steel roof too hot for cattle?
faq.a: A bare steel roof can be hot, so insulated sheets, a high roof and an open ridge are used to lower the heat.

blocks.title: Why Heat Is the Main Problem

blocks.text: Heat is the first problem for dairy animals in Pakistan. Summer temperatures are high, the air can be humid, and animals standing under a low or poorly ventilated roof suffer. A well-planned dairy shed design in Pakistan therefore starts with shade and moving air, and not with the number of animals. Cattle shed construction in Pakistan also has to deal with monsoon rain, dust and the daily washing of floors. A steel dairy shed can handle all of these if the roof, the sides and the floor are designed together. Steel Mind Engineers designs each shed around the animals' comfort and the farm's daily routine.

A high roof gives hot air room to rise above the animals. The eave height should leave enough space for the animals, for feed carts and for loaders, and the ridge should sit higher still. Steel Mind Engineers built the Dravton Dairy and Latifia Dairy sheds at 17 feet high. A pitched roof, which slopes to both sides, sheds rain quickly and creates a ridge along the top. That ridge is where you place the opening described next. If your farm uses insulated roof sheets, the roof also keeps the sun's heat away from the animals below.

Hot air is lighter than cool air, so it rises and collects under the roof. An open ridge, which is a continuous gap along the top of the roof with a cover above it, lets this air leave without any power. Fresh air enters from the sides to replace it. This simple stack effect works all day without electricity or fans. A ridge opening needs a cover so that rain does not enter, and the engineer designs that cover as part of the frame. Ridge ventilators and turbo vents can be added in sheds where more air movement is needed.

Open sides allow cross-flow of air through the shed. Where you need protection from driving rain, strong sun or wind, louvers do the job. A louver is a set of slats that lets air pass and keeps rain and direct sun out. Many farms combine the two, with open sides on the long walls and louvers on the weather side. The best choice depends on the wind direction at your site and the season. Tell the engineer where your site is and which side the monsoon wind comes from.

A dairy shed must stay dry. Floor slope and gutters carry manure, urine and wash water away from the animals, and a good roof gutter system moves rain away from the walls. Plan the drainage with your civil contractor before the steel is made, because the columns, the plinths and the floor level must agree. A wet, dirty floor raises the risk of infection and lameness and makes cleaning harder. Good drainage also protects the steel itself, because standing water at the column bases causes rust.

The frame spacing should match the feed alleys, the stalls and the milking area. If the frames are placed to suit the layout, columns do not block feeding lines or animal movement. A clear span, with no columns inside the width, gives the most freedom, while a multi-span shed places columns along the length of the middle. Steel Mind Engineers built a PEB dairy shed for Dravton Dairy at Chunian that is 115 feet wide and 342 feet long, and a PEB dairy shed for Latifia Dairy at Kasur that is 110 feet wide and 200 feet long. Both are examples of a layout planned around the farm.

blocks.title: The Milking Parlour and the Feed Store

blocks.text: A dairy farm is more than a cattle shed. The milking parlour is the place where the farm works every day, so it needs shade, clear floor space and good air. The feed store needs a tight roof, good sheet laps and ridge vents, because wet feed spoils fast. Steel Mind Engineers built a 21,686 square foot milking parlour shed, an 8,000 square foot feed storage shed and a rapid exit structure for Dravton Dairy at Chunian. Planning these buildings together saves money, because the same engineer can place the roads, the drains and the doors in one layout.

blocks.title: Build in Phases as the Herd Grows

blocks.text: A farm often grows over time, and steel makes growth easy. Bolted PEB frames allow extra bays at the end of a shed or a new shed beside the first. Dravton Dairy is an example: the farm has had four structures built at Chunian. When you plan the first shed, tell the engineer where the next one will stand, so that the end wall, the access road and the drains can be ready for it. Steel Mind Engineers can also coat the steel for damp, dirty air, which protects the frame for many years.
